tier_reason: Peer-reviewed PVLDB 19(2):224-237 paper; Table 1 (normalized to Redis) and Sec. 8 give 108x throughput, 0.25x latency, 257x checkpoint and 94x scale-out, and the load generator is public (benchmark/Resp.benchmark in the repo). It is not A because the paper names only the Azure VM SKU (F72s_v2), with no CPU model and no .NET/compiler version or flags.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Table 1 (normalized to Redis; the paper says Redis performs like Valkey and leaves it out of most runs, so the measured comparisons are against Valkey v8.1): node throughput 108x, latency at batch size 16 0.25x (4x lower), checkpoint speed 257x (Valkey 273.1s vs Garnet 1.06s), scale-out/migration speed 94x vs Valkey; memtier (1:9 SET:GET, 256M keys, 6400 clients): at least 20x higher throughput and 3x lower P99 latency than standalone Valkey, up to 40x/6x higher throughput than KeyDB/Dragonfly
corrections.stars_or_usage: 12k stars; the paper says Garnet is 'already widely deployed in large-scale scenarios across Microsoft'
corrections.caveats: Evaluation run and published by Garnet's own authors (all seven are Microsoft Research); the paper is peer-reviewed (PVLDB 19(2):224-237) but is not independent. Redis itself was mostly not run: the paper says open-source Redis performs like Valkey and uses Valkey v8.1 (plus KeyDB v6.3.4 and Dragonfly v1.29.0) as the measured baselines, so the 'normalized to Redis' ratios stand in for Redis. The CPU model is not given (only the Azure F72s_v2 SKU), and the .NET runtime version and build flags are not stated. memtier_benchmark became client-bottlenecked, so most headline figures come from Garnet's own Resp.bench tool. Language is C#, not C++.

notes: The record's caveat claiming Facebook/Meta-adjacent academic co-authors was wrong: all authors are Microsoft Research, and I corrected it. The measured baseline is Valkey v8.1 (a Redis fork) acting as the Redis proxy. The C++-only search filter returned a C# project.

tier_reason: First-party wiki page with JMH numbers against ConcurrentLinkedHashMap, Guava, Ehcache, Infinispan and java.util.LinkedHashMap LRU. The code is public (caffeine/src/jmh/.../GetPutBenchmark.java) and the CPU is stated, but the JVM version and flags are not. The rubric makes the project's own benchmark code with partial methodology C, not B; there is no peer-reviewed or independent third-party source.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Server-class (Xeon E5-2698B v3, 16 threads, bounded caches), GetPutBenchmark: 100% read 382.4M ops/s vs 313.9M (ConcurrentLinkedHashMap, ~1.2x) and 43.1M (Guava with concurrencyLevel 64, ~8.9x) (derived from page data); 75/25 read/write 279.4M vs 122.3M (~2.3x) and 37.3M (Guava-64, ~7.5x) (derived from page data); 100% write 48.3M vs 39.8M (~1.2x) (derived from page data). JDK LinkedHashMap LRU reaches only 13.6M/12.8M/10.9M ops/s in the same runs.
corrections.caveats: First-party numbers only. The exact JVM version and flags for the JMH run are not given. The server run is an old Azure G4 / Ubuntu 15.04 setup (the desktop run is on OS X Yosemite), so the figures date from roughly 2015 and an early Caffeine release. The Guava ratios use Guava tuned to concurrencyLevel 64; Guava's default does worse. Benchmark code is public (ComputeBenchmark.java, GetPutBenchmark.java under caffeine/src/jmh). Language is Java, not C++.

notes: All the figures match the server-class tables on the wiki; the ratios are computed and are now marked as derived. The C++-only search filter returned a Java project. The rubric's rule that own code with partial methodology is C forced the downgrade from B.

tier_reason: Peer-reviewed NSDI'21 paper (the abstract on the USENIX page and the full PDF) compares Segcache with Memcached 1.6.6: close to 8x speedup at 24 threads (over 70 vs 9 MQPS) and 5 vs 56 bytes of metadata per object. The CPU (dual Xeon Gold 6230R) and code (twitter/pelikan, thesys-lab/segcache) are given but the compiler and flags are not, so it is not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: NSDI'21 paper: close to 8x speedup over Memcached with 24 threads (Segcache over 70 MQPS vs Memcached 9 MQPS); up to 40% higher throughput than Memcached on a single thread; 5 bytes/object metadata vs Memcached's 56 bytes (91% less); 22-60% less memory than state-of-the-art designs (abstract), up to 60% less vs Memcached, and 42-88% less memory footprint vs Twitter's production PCache (slab) system
corrections.hardware: Dual-socket Intel Xeon Gold 6230R, 384GB DRAM, one 100Gbps NIC (dedicated hosts in Twitter's production fleet); closed-loop trace replay of the storage subsystem only
corrections.caveats: Paper numbers are for the original C Segcache module in twitter/pelikan (archived at thesys-lab/segcache), not the current Rust rewrite at pelikan-io/pelikan; the Rust README repeats them as properties of 'the same architecture'. The evaluation covers the storage subsystem only (the networking stack was not modified), uses Twitter production traces, and was run by Twitter/CMU authors. The compiler and flags are not stated. The README's '40-90% vs Pelikan's own slab storage' rounds the paper's 42-88% vs PCache. Language of the current repo is Rust, not C++.

notes: The numbers are now verified against the paper PDF (https://www.usenix.org/system/files/nsdi21-yang.pdf) rather than the blog, and hardware is filled in. Tier B holds, but the benchmarked code is the legacy C implementation (twitter/pelikan: 1,957 stars, last commit 2022-10-27), not the Rust repo. The C++-only search filter returned a Rust project.
